passage:
Tuesday: Vikas came home from a double shift and tripped over Nazia's school bag by the door. He shouted, loud enough for the neighbours, that she was careless and useless. Nazia went to her room and locked it.
Wednesday morning: He knocked before she left for school. "Last night I yelled at you and called you useless. That was wrong. I was tired, but that's not your fault, and it's not an excuse. I'm sorry." Nazia shrugged and walked out.
Saturday: Nazia sat on the arm of his chair while he watched cricket and said, casually, "You know, you're the only grown-up who says sorry like that." Then she told him about a fight with her friend.

qa.q: What did Vikas trip over?
qa.a: Nazia's school bag by the door.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt when Vikas apologised on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably still hurt and wary, which is why she shrugged, even if the apology mattered to her.

qa.q: Which part of Vikas's apology made it a real repair?
qa.a: He named exactly what he did and refused to use tiredness as an excuse.

qa.q: How does the Saturday talk show the effect of the repair on Nazia?
qa.a: She trusts him again enough to share a fight with her friend, showing the relationship survived his mistake.

grounding: Shows over several days a parent who shouted, then names it and apologises without excuses, and the teen's trust returning.

passage: Your Bidisha-phuppi was sixteen when I missed her school play. I had promised. Instead I stayed at the shop counting stock and told myself she wouldn't mind. She minded. She didn't speak to me for a week, and I, Rafiq, stubborn old fool, said she was being dramatic. Then one night I passed her room and saw the costume still on the chair. I knocked. I didn't say "but the shop" or "but I was busy". I said, "I broke a promise to you, and I pretended it didn't matter. It did. I'm sorry." She cried, and I cried. After that, she told me things. Mistakes don't end a family, beta. Hiding them does.

qa.q: What did Rafiq see on the chair in Bidisha's room?
qa.a: The costume.

qa.q: How was young Bidisha feeling during the week of silence?
qa.a: She was hurt and let down that Rafiq broke the promise and then called her dramatic.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Seeing the costume made Rafiq knock and apologise plainly, without mentioning the shop or being busy.

qa.q: How did the apology change things for Bidisha?
qa.a: She cried with Rafiq and afterwards began sharing things, trusting that the bond could survive the mistake.

grounding: Shows a parent who broke a promise returning to name it and apologise without excuses, teaching a teen that bonds survive mistakes.

passage: The day Damini came back from a year of hospital work in Mumbai, the monsoon flooded their lane in Kolhapur, and she and Tarun were stuck indoors with no power. For the first hour he played games on his phone and answered in grunts. She had missed his birthday call, his exam results and two parent meetings. By candlelight she sat down opposite him. "I wasn't there this year. I didn't call when I said I would, more than once. I'm not going to tell you it was all for the family. I'm sorry, Tarun." He kept his eyes on the screen. Then the battery died. He looked up. "You missed my results." "Tell me now?" she asked. The rain kept falling. He told her.

qa.q: What flooded their lane in Kolhapur?
qa.a: The monsoon.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling during the first hour?
qa.a: He was hurt and angry at her absence, hiding behind his phone and answering in grunts.

qa.q: Why was Damini's apology effective?
qa.a: She named what she missed, didn't hide behind excuses about the family, and then invited him to share instead of lecturing.

qa.q: What would change if Damini had said the work was all for Tarun's sake?
qa.a: Tarun would likely feel his hurt was dismissed, and the silence between them might have continued.

grounding: Illustrates a parent who was absent returning, naming what she missed and apologising without excuses.

passage: In her first year at the agricultural college in Dharwad, Swati apologised for everything and expected to be dropped by everyone. Growing up, her father's moods had decided whether home felt safe. Vaibhav-sir, her soil-science mentor, was dull in the best way: office hours every Tuesday, replies within a day, the same calm voice whether her samples were perfect or ruined. When she lost a whole batch to mould, she waited for the explosion. He said, "Happens. Let's see why." By third year she noticed something: when her roommate went quiet, Swati no longer assumed it was about her. She wrote in her notebook, "People can be steady. I can be too."

qa.q: What happened to Swati's batch of samples?
qa.a: She lost a whole batch to mould.

qa.q: What was Swati expecting when she lost the batch, and why?
qa.a: She was afraid of an explosion, because her father's moods had made home feel unsafe.

qa.q: What helped Swati become more secure?
qa.a: Vaibhav-sir's steady reliability over time, plus her own reflection on how her past shaped her expectations.

qa.q: How might Swati's roommate experience the change in her?
qa.a: The roommate probably finds Swati calmer and easier to be around, since quiet moments no longer feel like a threat to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult with an insecure past becoming more secure through a steady mentor and reflecting on old patterns.

passage: Zanele had moved between three aunties' houses before she was twelve, and in her first year at university in Cape Town she kept friendships at arm's length, ready to leave first. Selin, her lab partner, didn't seem to notice the walls. She saved Zanele a seat every Monday, texted when she said she would, and remembered her exams. When Zanele snapped at her over a lost file, Selin said, "That stung. Coffee later?" and meant it. Zanele also started seeing a counsellor on campus, drawing a map of all those houses. By second year she caught herself texting Selin first, without rehearsing. "I think I'm learning people come back," she told the counsellor, surprised.

qa.q: How many aunties' houses had Zanele moved between?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when she caught herself texting Selin first?
qa.a: She felt surprised and more trusting, starting to believe people come back.

qa.q: Which two things helped Zanele change?
qa.a: Selin's steady reliability and the counsellor helping her reflect on her past moves.

qa.q: What is it like for Selin when Zanele snaps at her?
qa.a: Selin feels stung but stays warm, naming the hurt and still offering coffee.

grounding: Illustrates earned security through a reliable friend and a counsellor who helps a young adult reflect on past patterns.

passage: In the counselling centre's small blue room, Anjali watched the clock the way she always had, waiting for Leela to get bored of her. It was their twentieth session. Leela had never once been late, never cancelled without a week's warning, and hadn't flinched when Anjali shouted in session six. Today Anjali said, "My mother used to disappear for days. I think I test everyone to see if they'll do the same." Leela nodded. "And what have you noticed here?" Anjali was quiet. "You keep coming back. It's boring, actually." They both laughed. Walking out past the reception desk, Anjali noticed she hadn't looked at the clock once.

qa.q: Which session was it?
qa.a: Their twentieth session.

qa.q: What was Anjali afraid of when she watched the clock?
qa.a: She feared Leela would get bored and leave, the way her mother used to disappear.

qa.q: What made Leela's help work over time?
qa.a: Her steady reliability and questions that helped Anjali reflect on her pattern of testing people.

qa.q: How might Leela see Anjali's joke about it being boring?
qa.a: Leela likely sees it as a sign of growing trust, since Anjali is noticing that reliability is real.

grounding: Shows a young adult gaining security through a therapist's reliability and reflection on childhood patterns.

passage: For a while I had the perfect excuse. I'd read one article and decided: I'm Karthik, and I'm avoidant. So when my friend Pankaj's father was in hospital and I didn't call for a week, I told myself, that's just my attachment style. Pankaj didn't buy it. He said, "You're not a label. You're my friend who went missing." That hit hard. Now I think of it more like weather: I do pull back when things get heavy, especially with family stuff, less with teammates. Knowing that helps me catch it. It doesn't let me off. So I called him, apologised without the jargon, and drove him to the hospital on Sunday.

qa.q: What did Karthik do on Sunday?
qa.a: Drove Pankaj to the hospital.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when Pankaj said "You're my friend who went missing"?
qa.a: Karthik felt stung and ashamed, realising the label had been used as an excuse.

qa.q: What is the wiser way Karthik now uses the idea of attachment style?
qa.a: As a tendency that helps notice when pulling back starts, while still taking responsibility and showing up.

qa.q: How did Pankaj experience Karthik's week of silence?
qa.a: Pankaj felt let down by a missing friend while his father was in hospital, and would not accept the label as an excuse.

grounding: Shows a young adult who stops using an attachment label as an excuse and treats it as a tendency while taking responsibility.

passage: I'm Chetan, Bhavna's classmate on the design course, and I've watched her change this year. In first year, if her boyfriend didn't text back, she'd tell us, "I'm anxiously attached, I can't help it," and send twenty messages. This term something shifted. I overheard her in the canteen telling a friend, "Yeah, I lean anxious, mostly with him, not with you lot. But that's not his job to fix." During our group critique she put her phone in her bag and didn't touch it for an hour. When she snapped at a junior over a model, she went back and apologised. I don't know what goes on inside her head. But she seems to use the words to understand herself, not to hide.

qa.q: How long did Bhavna leave her phone in her bag during the critique?
qa.a: For an hour.

qa.q: What might Bhavna be feeling when she says "that's not his job to fix"?
qa.a: She seems more settled and responsible, less panicked, owning her anxious tendency instead of blaming it.

qa.q: What does Bhavna do that shows she takes responsibility for her behaviour?
qa.a: She puts the phone away during the critique and goes back to apologise after snapping at a junior.

qa.q: How does Chetan see the change in Bhavna?
qa.a: Chetan notices she now uses the words to understand herself rather than as an excuse, while admitting not knowing her inner thoughts.

grounding: Shows through a classmate's eyes a person treating attachment style as a context-dependent tendency, not an excuse.

passage:
Week one, a Monday: When Maria asked why Ayesha had ignored her texts all weekend, Ayesha shrugged. "I'm avoidant. It's how I'm wired." Maria went quiet and left for class.
Week three, a Thursday: Ayesha noticed she answered her cricket teammates within minutes but froze when her roommate wrote anything personal. So it wasn't everyone, all the time.
Week four, a Sunday: She knocked on Maria's door. "I used that word like a shield. I do pull away when things get personal, but ignoring you was my choice, and it was unkind. I'm sorry." Maria moved her laundry off the bed so Ayesha could sit.

qa.q: How quickly did Ayesha answer her cricket teammates?
qa.a: Within minutes.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel when she knocked on Maria's door?
qa.a: She seemed humbled and sorry, ready to own that ignoring Maria was her choice.

qa.q: What did Ayesha notice that changed how she saw the label?
qa.a: That she only froze with personal messages, so the tendency depended on context rather than being fixed.

qa.q: How does Maria show her response to the apology?
qa.a: She moves her laundry so Ayesha can sit, showing she is willing to reconnect.

grounding: Shows across weeks a young adult moving from using an attachment label as an excuse to seeing it as a tendency and taking responsibility.

subtype: Patterns triggered by a partner's style [Observer]
passage: When I was twenty-five, beta, I lived with my brother Uday and his new wife, Kamini, in a tiny Delhi flat. I watched them every evening like a play. Kamini would ask, "Why so quiet?" Uday would say, "Nothing," and pick up the paper. She'd ask again, louder. He'd go for a walk. She'd cry. He'd stay out longer. Each made the other worse, and each told me the other was the problem. One night I, Alka, the nosy sister, drew it on the back of an envelope: arrows going round and round. "It's not you, and it's not you," I said. "It's this circle." They laughed, then went very quiet. Kamini started asking once; Uday started coming back in ten minutes. That drawing stayed on their fridge for years.

qa.q: What did Alka draw on the back of the envelope?
qa.a: Arrows going round and round.

qa.q: What was young Alka feeling as she watched them every evening?
qa.a: She was worried and frustrated, seeing both of them hurting and blaming each other.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Alka's drawing showed the loop as a shared circle, so each could change their own part.

qa.q: How might Uday have felt when Kamini asked again, louder?
qa.a: Uday likely felt pressured and overwhelmed, so he withdrew on a walk, which made Kamini more upset.

grounding: Shows an observer who sees a pursue-withdraw loop and helps the couple see it as a shared pattern, not one person's fault.

subtype: Patterns triggered by a partner's style [Observer]
passage: The tyre burst forty kilometres from Nainital, in the rain, and Ramesh stood by the car with his friends Usha and Deven while the driver changed it. Within ten minutes they were at it again. Usha: "You didn't check the tyres, did you? You never tell me anything." Deven turned away and stared at the valley. Usha followed him, voice rising. Deven walked further. Ramesh, holding the umbrella, had seen this loop all trip, at breakfast, at the hotel desk. Later, in the dhaba, he said carefully, "Can I say something? When Usha pushes, Deven pulls away, and then Usha pushes harder. You're both stuck on the same wheel." They looked at each other. Deven said, "I do go quiet." Usha said, "And I chase." The rest of the drive felt lighter.

qa.q: Where were they when the tyre burst?
qa.a: Forty kilometres from Nainital, in the rain.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling as he watched the loop repeat all trip?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and concerned, careful about how to say what he had seen.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh's words help?
qa.a: He described the pattern as a shared wheel, so neither Usha nor Deven had to be the one at fault.

qa.q: How might Deven feel when Usha follows him with a rising voice?
qa.a: Deven probably feels cornered and overwhelmed, so he walks further away.

grounding: Illustrates an observer naming a pursue-withdraw loop between two partners as a shared pattern, which eases the conflict.

subtype: Patterns triggered by a partner's style [Observer]
passage: From the sofa in their shared Pune flat, Vasudha could hear it through the wall again: Dilnaz on the phone to Joel, "Why didn't you call at lunch?", then a long pause, then "Say something!" Then the call ending, Dilnaz crying, and twenty minutes later another call. Vasudha knew Joel from college. He wasn't cruel, just the kind who went still when things got loud. And the stiller he got, the louder Dilnaz got. On Sunday, over poha, Vasudha said, "I don't think either of you is the villain. It's like a see-saw: you push, he freezes, you push harder." Dilnaz put her spoon down. "So it's my fault?" "No. It's the see-saw. You could both step off." That night Dilnaz texted Joel: "Can we talk about the pattern, not about who's wrong?"

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Dilnaz eat on Sunday?
qa.a: Poha.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she listened through the wall?
qa.a: She felt worried for Dilnaz and sad, seeing the calls go round in circles.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do well when she spoke to Dilnaz?
qa.a: She described a shared see-saw instead of blaming one person, which let Dilnaz reframe the problem.

qa.q: How might Joel react to Dilnaz's text about the pattern?
qa.a: Joel may feel relieved and less attacked, since the message is about the pattern, not about who is wrong.

grounding: Shows an observer helping a friend see an anxious-avoidant loop as a shared pattern rather than one person's fault.

passage: The science test came back with 14 out of 20 in red, and Rekha folded it into a tiny square before anyone could see. All the way home in the school van she stared out of the window. At dinner she said she wasn't hungry. "Everyone got more than me. I'm the stupid one now," she told her elder brother, Sumit, when he found her crying on the balcony. "Last week you were the genius," he said. "Last week I got 19." Sumit sat down beside her. "So you're only good when the number's big?" Rekha didn't answer. She pressed the paper square tighter in her fist.

qa.q: What mark did Rekha get in the science test?
qa.a: 14 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel about herself after the test?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and worthless, as if one lower mark proved she was stupid.

qa.q: How could Sumit or her parents help Rekha next?
qa.a: Show her she is valued whatever the mark, and talk about what she learned rather than the number.

qa.q: What might Sumit be thinking when he asks if she's only good when the number's big?
qa.a: He seems concerned that Rekha's sense of worth depends entirely on marks.

grounding: Shows a child whose sense of worth rises and falls with marks, crumbling after an ordinary poor result.

passage:
"Mumma, I came second."
"Second in the whole district drawing contest, Sumit! That's wonderful."
"It's not. Rishabh came first. So mine was worse."
Neelam put down the ladle. "Yours was a tiger in the rain. I loved the stripes."
"Nobody cares about second. You only put first-prize ones on the fridge."
"Did I say that?"
"You put Didi's gold certificate there."
Neelam was quiet. "Hmm. I did."
"If I'm not first, I'm nothing." Sumit kicked the chair leg. "I'm never entering again."

qa.q: What did Sumit draw?
qa.a: A tiger in the rain.

qa.q: Why did Sumit say "If I'm not first, I'm nothing"?
qa.a: He feels worthless and disappointed, believing only first place earns love and attention.

qa.q: What could Neelam do now to help?
qa.a: Praise the effort and ideas in the tiger drawing and display it too, so Sumit sees his worth isn't tied to winning.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel when Sumit mentions the fridge?
qa.a: Neelam seems surprised and uneasy, realising her own habit may have taught him that only winners count.

grounding: Illustrates a child who feels valued only when winning and crumbles after coming second.

passage: Last term I got 62 out of 100 in maths, and I didn't tell anyone for two days. I'm Ganga, and I'm the one who always gets the highest marks in our class. That's who I am. Or that's who I thought I was. When the paper came back, it felt like the ground had gone. I stopped talking in class. I didn't go for kho-kho. My friend Hansa asked what was wrong and I snapped at her. At home I tore out the page and hid it in my old pencil box. When Hansa said she'd got 58 and was fine, I couldn't understand how. For me, one bad mark felt like proof I wasn't good at all.

qa.q: Where did Ganga hide the page?
qa.a: In the old pencil box.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when the paper came back?
qa.a: Ganga felt crushed and ashamed, as if the ground had gone, because being top felt like Ganga's whole worth.

qa.q: What could help Ganga see a bad mark differently?
qa.a: Hearing from adults and friends that worth doesn't depend on marks, and treating the paper as a chance to learn.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Ganga snapped?
qa.a: Hansa was probably hurt and puzzled, since she only asked what was wrong.

grounding: Shows a child whose worth depends on top marks, so one ordinary setback feels like proof of not being enough.

passage: The power went out at eight, two hours before Joseph's science model had to be finished, and the little wind turbine still wouldn't spin. By candlelight he tried a smaller blade, then bent the wire, then taped on cardboard fins, muttering. Shalini held the torch. At half past nine the blades gave one slow turn. "It barely moves," Joseph said, face falling. "The winners will have motors." Shalini set the torch down. "I watched you try four different blades in the dark without giving up. When one failed, you changed the angle instead of starting over. That's how engineers think." Joseph looked at the turbine again. "Next year I'll try a gear," he said, already sketching.

qa.q: What time did the power go out?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: How was Joseph feeling when the blades gave one slow turn?
qa.a: He felt disappointed, comparing it to winners with motors.

qa.q: What kind of praise did Shalini give, and why does it help?
qa.a: She praised his persistence and strategy, not the result, which shows him his worth isn't about winning.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini to watch Joseph start sketching a gear?
qa.a: Shalini is probably pleased and relieved, seeing that her praise for his effort made him want to try something harder.

grounding: Shows a parent praising effort and strategy rather than results, so the child feels safe to try hard things.

passage: Neelam walked off the stage of the school hall in Lucknow with her cheeks burning. She had spelled "rhythm" with one h and gone out in the third round. Jyoti-ma'am found her behind the curtain, pulling at her sleeve. "I got out so early. I'm hopeless at spelling." Jyoti-ma'am crouched down. "I saw you practise with flashcards every lunch for two weeks. And when Farhan froze on stage, you whispered 'breathe' to him. That was kind." Neelam sniffed. "But I didn't win." "You tried something hard in front of three hundred people. Want to learn the tricky words with me for next year?" Neelam, after a moment, nodded.

qa.q: Which word did Neelam misspell?
qa.a: "rhythm", with one h.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling behind the curtain?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hopeless after going out early.

qa.q: What did Jyoti-ma'am praise, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Her practice, her kindness to Farhan and her courage, which shows her worth isn't only about winning.

qa.q: If you were Farhan, how might you feel about Neelam's whisper?
qa.a: Grateful and less alone, since someone helped in a scary moment.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher praising effort and kindness after a loss, helping a child risk trying again.

passage:
"I lost all five games, Ammi. All five."
Parveen handed him a glass of water. "You played five full games against bigger kids. How did it feel to keep going?"
"Terrible." Hrithik slumped on the bench. "Sameer won everything. He's a genius."
"I noticed something in your third game. You stopped and thought for a long time before moving your knight."
"I was trying to protect my queen."
"And did it work?"
"For a bit. Then I got scared and rushed."
"So you've found your next thing to practise: slowing down when you're scared. That's a real strategy."
Hrithik thought. "Can we play at home tonight? Slowly?"
"Slowly. And I'll probably lose."

qa.q: How many games did Hrithik lose?
qa.a: All five games.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling after the tournament?
qa.a: He felt terrible and defeated, comparing himself with Sameer.

qa.q: How did Parveen turn the loss into something useful?
qa.a: By noticing his careful thinking with the knight and naming a strategy to practise, instead of focusing on results.

qa.q: Why might Parveen say she will probably lose?
qa.a: She wants Hrithik to enjoy practising without pressure, showing that losing is ordinary and not a measure of worth.

grounding: Shows a parent praising strategy and effort after losses, so the child is willing to keep trying.

passage:
Monday. Everyone went for the school musical auditions today. I said musicals are for losers and sat in the back row doing impressions of Pallavi's high note till people laughed. She went red. I felt great for about a minute. Truth, since nobody reads this: I've been practising that same song in the bathroom for a month. My voice cracks on the chorus. If I went up and it cracked in front of everyone, I think I'd die. Mocking is safer. But Pallavi got called back, and I'm sitting here feeling rubbish. Ms Rao said anyone can come to the open practice on Thursday, no audience. Maybe.
Ayesha

qa.q: How long has Ayesha been practising the song?
qa.a: For a month.

qa.q: What is Ayesha afraid of under the mocking?
qa.a: Ayesha is afraid of the voice cracking in front of everyone and being exposed as failing.

qa.q: What could help Ayesha more than a lecture?
qa.a: Going to Thursday's open practice with no audience, a safe place to try and even fail.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when people laughed at the impression?
qa.a: Pallavi was likely embarrassed and hurt, going red in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a teen mocking others and refusing to try, with bravado hiding a fear of being seen to fail.

passage: At the village school in Moga, Amandeep was the loudest boy on the bench. When Eshaan missed his serve at the volleyball trial, Amandeep hooted, "My grandmother serves better!" and the others laughed. But when the PT master called his name, Amandeep stayed seated. "Volleyball is boring. I don't need trials. Everyone knows I'm the best." The master looked at him a long moment. After practice, Eshaan found him behind the water tank, flicking stones. "You were scared," Eshaan said. Amandeep started to deny it, then didn't. "What if I miss too? They'll laugh." "Like you laughed at me," Eshaan said. Then, more kindly: "Come early tomorrow. Just us. No one watching."

qa.q: Where did Eshaan find Amandeep after practice?
qa.a: Behind the water tank, flicking stones.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when he stayed seated?

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when Amandeep hooted at his serve?

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m. Posted the photo from Irawati's party at seven. Forty-one likes. Irawati's got three hundred in an hour. I've checked it about fifty times. Deleted it at ten, because forty-one looked pathetic next to hers. Scrolled through everyone's holidays: Irawati in the hills, two seniors at some beach, and me in this room with a leaking tap. passage: In the kasba near Satara, the network was only strong on the roof of the post office, so Madhuri climbed up there every evening to scroll. Girls from Mumbai with perfect skin, cafés and trips abroad. Her own face, in the phone's camera, looked dull and dusty. She had started asking her cousin Madhav, "Do I look too village?" before every photo. Last Saturday her picture of the temple fair got only nine likes, and she skipped dinner. But on Sunday, at the district relay, she ran the last leg and pulled her team from third to first. Madhav lifted her onto his shoulders. The whole kasba cheered. That evening she didn't climb the post office roof at all.

qa.q: Where was the network strong in the kasba?
qa.a: On the roof of the post office.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel about herself while scrolling?
qa.a: She felt dull and behind, comparing her face and life to girls from Mumbai.

qa.q: What gave Madhuri firmer ground than likes?
qa.a: Running the last leg at the district relay and winning with her team.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt lifting Madhuri onto his shoulders?
qa.a: Madhav was likely proud and happy for her, sharing in the win.

grounding: Shows a teen measuring herself against curated images and likes, finding firmer ground in an offline achievement.

passage: On the way back from the tuition centre in Sitapur, Charu kicked the dust and said again, "I'm useless at everything." It was the fourth time that week Raghav had heard it. That afternoon she had refused the teacher's offer to present their water-filter model at the block science fair. "Let Raghav do it. I'll mess up." Raghav knew she'd built most of it. He stopped under the neem tree. "You worked out the charcoal layer. I didn't even know charcoal could clean water." She shrugged. He walked her home every day that week. On Friday, when she said she felt low all the time and wasn't sleeping, he said, "Let's tell Kamla-didi at the health centre, now. I'll come." That evening Kamla-didi sat with them on the bench outside the centre and listened.

qa.q: What did Charu refuse to present?
qa.a: Their water-filter model at the block science fair.

qa.q: What was Raghav thinking when Charu said "Let Raghav do it"?
qa.a: He felt concerned and a little frustrated, knowing she'd built most of the model.

qa.q: Which of Raghav's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Taking her to Kamla-didi that same day, because her low mood had lasted and needed a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Raghav praises the charcoal layer?
qa.a: Charu might feel noticed but unable to believe it yet, which is why she shrugged.

grounding: Illustrates a friend hearing constant put-downs, giving specific praise, staying close and involving a trusted adult.

passage: Jamal had known Rania since they were nine, at the same Birmingham school. Lately she said "I'm so thick" after every answer, even right ones. When the art teacher offered her a place in the city exhibition, Rania said no before the teacher had finished the sentence. Jamal waited till they were at the bus stop. "The bird you painted, the one with the torn wing, people stopped in the corridor to look at it. I did too." Rania rolled her eyes, but she didn't change the subject. He sat with her at lunch every day that week, not fixing anything. On Friday he said, "You've seemed low for ages. Would you talk to Ms Okafor? I'll wait outside her door." Rania thought for a long moment, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Rania paint?
qa.a: A bird with a torn wing.

qa.q: What was Jamal feeling as he watched Rania turn down the exhibition?
qa.a: He was worried and sad, seeing her put herself down and miss a real chance.

qa.q: What did Jamal do that could help Rania?
qa.a: He gave specific praise, stayed close at lunch and encouraged her to talk to Ms Okafor, offering to wait outside.

qa.q: How might Rania see Jamal's offer to wait outside the door?
qa.a: She may feel supported and less scared, knowing she won't face the talk alone.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing low self-worth, sharing specific praise, staying close and encouraging a trusted adult.

passage: At the design agency, Sunaina's intern desk sat next to Karthik's, which was handy, because she asked him about everything. "Is this font okay? Should I say 'Hi' or 'Dear'? Do you think the client will like the blue?" He answered, patiently, eleven times before lunch. At the afternoon review, the creative head said, "The layout's good; the headline's weak." Sunaina nodded, went to the washroom and cried for twenty minutes. The praise had already evaporated; only "weak" remained. Back at her desk she started typing a message to Karthik: "Do you think she hates my work?" Then she stopped, deleted it, and wrote on a sticky note: "What do I think of the headline?"

qa.q: What did the creative head say at the review?
qa.a: "The layout's good; the headline's weak."

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel after the review?
qa.a: She felt crushed and upset, crying for twenty minutes, because the mild criticism outweighed the praise.

qa.q: What small step did Sunaina take towards an inner sense of worth?
qa.a: She deleted the message asking Karthik and wrote a note asking what she herself thought of the headline.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel after answering eleven questions before lunch?
qa.a: Karthik is patient but may feel a bit tired, and might worry that Sunaina doubts her own judgement.

grounding: Shows a young adult who asks for approval before every choice and is crushed by mild criticism, starting to build inner worth.

passage:
Dear Joseph-sir,
You once told our Class 12 that I'd go far because I "always ask good questions". I've been thinking about that. In college I ask questions about everything, but mostly one: "Is this okay?" I send my roommate my assignments before I submit. I ask three friends which shirt to wear to a seminar. Last week a professor wrote "argument unclear" next to one paragraph, and I didn't sleep. The good comments above it didn't count at all. It's like praise wears off in an hour and I need more. So I've started a small experiment: one decision a day with no asking. Today it was the shirt. It was fine. I thought you'd like to know.
Kishore

qa.q: What did the professor write next to one paragraph?
qa.a: "argument unclear"

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after the professor's comment?
qa.a: Kishore felt so upset and anxious that sleep wouldn't come, while the good comments seemed to count for nothing.

qa.q: Why is Kishore's small experiment a good step?
qa.a: Making one decision a day without asking slowly builds trust in Kishore's own judgement.

qa.q: How might Joseph-sir feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Joseph-sir would likely feel touched to be trusted and glad Kishore is working on it.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who needs approval for every decision and is crushed by mild criticism, beginning to build inner worth.

passage: You'll laugh, but I asked six people whether I should cut my hair. Six. That's how all of first year went for me. I'm Manoj, by the way, twenty, and I couldn't choose a lunch order without checking what my friend Avni was getting. When she said, gently, that my presentation was "a bit long", I went home feeling like the floor had dropped away. Three hours of replaying it. A compliment from her lasted, what, a morning? Then I needed another. The college counsellor said something I keep thinking about: "Approval from outside is like sugar. Sweet, and then it's gone." So now I practise. Small things. I chose this shirt myself. I actually like it.

qa.q: How many people did Manoj ask about the haircut?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel after Avni called the presentation a bit long?
qa.a: Manoj felt crushed, as if the floor had dropped away, replaying it for three hours.

qa.q: What is Manoj doing to build an inner sense of worth?
qa.a: Practising small choices alone, like picking a shirt, after the counsellor's advice about outside approval.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt if she knew her gentle comment caused three hours of replaying?
qa.a: Avni might feel surprised and sorry, since she meant it kindly.

grounding: Shows a young adult for whom approval fades quickly and mild criticism crushes, practising small independent choices.
